Bus-Route Survey: Equation Traceability

Source: vignettes/bus-route-equations.Rmd
bus-route-equations.Rmd

Overview

This page maps each formula in tidycreel’s bus-route estimators to its published source and to the function that computes it. It is a reference for checking the implementation, not a tutorial; the bus-route How-to page shows the workflow.

The sources, and what each supplies:

  • Robson & Jones (1989) define the bus-route design and its effort estimator: the crew visits every site on each pass, waits a scheduled time at each, and expands what it sees by the circuit time over the wait (their Eq. 12).
  • Pollock, Jones & Brown (1994, section 15.5.3) give the same estimator as Eq. 15.10 (effort) and 15.11 (catch), with worked examples in Tables 15.14–15.17.
  • Jones & Pollock (2012, Eq. 19.4–19.5, pp. 911–912) give the general Horvitz–Thompson totals, Ê=∑ei/πi\hat{E} = \sum e_i/\pi_i and Ĥ=∑hi/πi\hat{H} = \sum h_i/\pi_i, “where πi\pi_i is the total probability that the ith sampling unit is included in the sample”. tidycreel writes the bus-route estimator in this form.
  • Hoenig et al. (1997) supply the estimator for anglers interviewed mid-trip.

Code references below name functions, not line numbers, which go stale.

1. Site Weight and Inclusion Probability

Formula:

πi=p_sitei×p_period\pi_i = p\_site_i \times p\_period

p_period is the probability that the sampled period (for example the morning or the afternoon) is the one worked; it is constant within a circuit. p_site is the site’s weight within the circuit, given in one of two ways:

Argument(s) p_site Constraint Design
wait_time, circuit_time wi/Tw_i / T waits add up to no more than TT bus route: every site visited on each pass
p_site as given adds up to 1 within a circuit a randomly chosen site on each pass

For a bus route, wiw_i is the scheduled wait at site ii and TT “the total time to complete a full circuit of the route, including traveling and waiting” (Pollock et al. 1994, p. 238). A party at the site can be seen only while the crew is there, so wi/Tw_i/T is the share of the period during which it can be observed. The shares add up to less than 1 whenever the route has travel time. Rescaling them to add up to 1 divides by the total wait instead of TT, and lowers every total by the travelling share of the circuit (GH #539).

R implementation: creel_design() computes .p_site (from waits) and .pi_i in the sampling frame and checks the constraints; add_interviews() joins .pi_i to each interview by site and circuit.

2. Enumeration Expansion

Formula:

expansioni=n_countedin_interviewedi\text{expansion}_i = \frac{n\_counted_i}{n\_interviewed_i}

When not every party at a site is interviewed, the interviewed parties stand for those that were not. With every party interviewed, the expansion is 1, as in the examples below.

R implementation: add_interviews() stores .expansion. Two edge cases:

  • Nobody seen (0/00/0): the site-visit contributes zero effort, because no party was there; estimate_effort() sets it to 0 deliberately.
  • Parties seen, none interviewed (n_counted>0n\_counted > 0, n_interviewed=0n\_interviewed = 0): the expansion is undefined and add_interviews() warns. Their effort and catch are unknown, not zero, so the effort, catch, harvest and release totals stop with an error that names each such site-day. Remove those rows to leave the parties out deliberately, or impute their values and set n_interviewed to the number of parties the values stand for. The same refusal covers a missing count or a missing value on an interviewed row.

3. Effort

Formula (Jones & Pollock 2012, Eq. 19.4):

Ê=∑ieiπi,ei=ai×expansioni\hat{E} = \sum_{i} \frac{e_i}{\pi_i}, \qquad e_i = a_i \times \text{expansion}_i

where aia_i is interview ii’s angler effort: the hours fished times n_anglers, or the hours fished alone when no party size is given. Pollock et al. write πj\pi_j for the probability of the sampled period, tidycreel’s p_period. With πi=(wi/T)πj\pi_i = (w_i/T)\,\pi_j the sum is their Eq. 15.10 term for term:

Ê=T∑i1wi∑jejiπj\hat{E} = T \sum_i \frac{1}{w_i} \sum_j \frac{e_{ji}}{\pi_j}

Unit: angler-hours when add_interviews() was given n_anglers; party-hours when it was not (it warns). The effort column is read as hours.

R implementation: estimate_effort() dispatches to estimate_effort_br(), which forms .e_i and .contribution =ei/πi= e_i/\pi_i and sums them. get_site_contributions() returns the per-interview table.

4. Catch, Harvest and Release Totals

Formula (Jones & Pollock 2012, Eq. 19.5; Pollock et al. 1994, Eq. 15.11):

Ĥ=∑ihiπi,hi=harvesti×expansioni\hat{H} = \sum_i \frac{h_i}{\pi_i}, \qquad h_i = \text{harvest}_i \times \text{expansion}_i

and likewise for catch and released fish. These totals are Horvitz–Thompson totals of the fish themselves. They are not effort times a rate, so they need no assumption about the covariance of the two.

R implementation: estimate_total_catch(), estimate_total_harvest() and estimate_total_release() dispatch to estimate_total_catch_br(), estimate_total_harvest_br() and estimate_total_release_br(), which share br_build_estimates().

5. Rates from Complete Trips

Eq. 19.4 and 19.5 are totals; the sources define no separate bus-route rate. The rate this design supports is the ratio of the two totals:

HPUÊ=ĤÊ=∑ihi/πi∑iei/πi\widehat{\text{HPUE}} = \frac{\hat{H}}{\hat{E}} = \frac{\sum_i h_i/\pi_i}{\sum_i e_i/\pi_i}

This is a ratio of means, reported as method = "ratio-of-means-hpue" (or -cpue, -rpue). Its unit follows the denominator: fish per angler-hour, or per party-hour without n_anglers.

Variance. survey::svyratio() linearises numerator and denominator together. The two totals come from the same interviews and are strongly positively correlated, so dividing two separately estimated totals and treating them as independent overstates the SE.

R implementation: estimate_harvest_rate(), estimate_catch_rate() and estimate_release_rate() dispatch to estimate_harvest_br() (catch and release reuse it with their own column), whose ratio step is br_harvest_rate_estimates(). On a bus-route design use_trips defaults to "complete".

6. Rates from Incomplete Trips

Anglers interviewed mid-trip need a different estimator, selected with use_trips = "incomplete".

Hoenig, Jones, Pollock, Robson & Wade (1997) compare the two candidates under roving-type sampling: encounter probability proportional to time fished, and catch observed only up to the interview. Writing CjC_j for the catch and LjL_j for the hours fished by angler jj at the time of interview, the ratio of means has expectation (their Eq. 3.2)

E[R1]≈∑jλjLj*2∑jLj*2E[R_1] \;\approx\; \frac{\sum_j \lambda_j L_j^{*2}}{\sum_j L_j^{*2}}

a weighting of individual rates λj\lambda_j by the square of completed trip length Lj*L_j^{*}. So R1R_1 “does not provide an estimate of catch rate that can be used with an independent estimate of total effort to provide an unbiased estimate of total catch except in the unrealistic case where λ\lambda is constant over all anglers.” The mean of ratios has approximately the correct expectation.

On a bus route the interviews are not equally likely, so each enters a Hájek weighted mean:

HPUÊinc=∑iwi(hi/ai)∑iwi,wi=expansioniπi×n_anglersi\widehat{\text{HPUE}}_{\text{inc}} \;=\; \frac{\sum_i w_i \, (h_i / a_i)}{\sum_i w_i}, \qquad w_i = \frac{\text{expansion}_i}{\pi_i} \times n\_anglers_i

where aia_i is angler-effort. The n_anglersin\_anglers_i factor applies when party size varies: an interview is a party, the rate is per angler, and meeting a party meets all its anglers (GH #513). It is reported as method = "mean-of-ratios-hpue".

Truncation. The mean of ratios has infinite asymptotic variance as trip length goes to zero. Hoenig et al. recommend disregarding trips shorter than 30 minutes, which is the truncate_at = 0.5 default. The threshold applies to elapsed trip duration, not to angler-hours: a party of five fishing twelve minutes supplies a full angler-hour and is still the unstable case. truncate_at = NULL disables truncation and warns.

use_trips = "diagnostic" returns both rates. They are different estimators, each the one its trip type supports, but both divide by the same effort column, so they share a unit (per angler-hour with n_anglers, per party-hour without) and the gap between them reflects trip status rather than a change of unit.

R implementation: br_incomplete_harvest_rate(), called from estimate_harvest_br().

7. Variance and What the Total Covers

Design. The per-interview contributions are analysed as a stratified sample with the sampled day as the primary sampling unit, stratified by the design’s strata. Interviews on the same day share that day’s conditions, so they are not independent draws (GH #198).

Method. survey::svytotal() for totals and survey::svyratio() for rates, by Taylor linearisation (Lumley 2010); variance = "bootstrap" or "jackknife" replicate the same design. A stratum with one sampled day has no between-day variance and is refused.

Within-day variance. Robson & Jones (1989, p. 95) show that with one crew per route per day the within-day component cannot be estimated separately. The day-level variance contains it, so the SE includes it, but tidycreel reports no separate within-day term for bus routes.

Target. The total covers the sampled days. Robson & Jones (Eq. 13) expand the mean daily estimate to all NN days of a stratum; tidycreel does not implement that expansion for bus routes, and target = "stratum_total" or "period_total" is refused rather than ignored (GH #520). The result records effort_target = "sampled_days".

R implementation: br_add_psu_key() sets the PSU; get_variance_design() applies the variance method.

8. Worked Check: Pollock et al. (1994), Tables 15.15–15.17

Pollock et al. give one day of direct-expansion interviews on a five-site route: a 360-minute circuit with waits of 30, 30, 15, 60 and 60 minutes, and the morning or afternoon chosen with probability 0.5. Site 3 had no anglers. They report Ê=24,814.80\hat{E} = 24{,}814.80 minutes (Table 15.16) and Ĉ=227.88\hat{C} = 227.88 fish (Table 15.17).

A design needs two sampled days for a between-day variance, so the published day is entered twice. Each day’s estimate is then the published one, and the sampled-day total is twice it. Trip durations are converted to hours.

library(tidycreel)

frame <- data.frame(
  site = as.character(1:5),
  circuit = "am_pm",
  wait_min = c(30, 30, 15, 60, 60),
  circuit_min = 360
)

one_day <- data.frame(
  site = c("1", "1", "2", "2", "4", "4", "4", "5"),
  trip_min = c(135, 165, 175, 215, 150, 145, 168, 225),
  catch = c(3, 2, 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 1)
)
days <- as.Date(c("2024-06-01", "2024-06-02"))
interviews <- do.call(rbind, lapply(days, function(d) cbind(date = d, one_day)))
interviews$day_type <- "weekday"
interviews$circuit <- "am_pm"
interviews$trip_hours <- interviews$trip_min / 60
interviews$trip_status <- "complete"
# Every party at a site was interviewed.
interviews$n_counted <- ave(rep(1L, nrow(interviews)), interviews$date, interviews$site,
  FUN = length
)
interviews$n_interviewed <- interviews$n_counted

Pollock et al.’s estimate is party effort, the trip length of each party, so the interviews are added without n_anglers. add_interviews() warns that it is assuming one angler per interview, and the estimates are labelled party-hours, which is what this example is.

design <- creel_design(
  data.frame(date = days, day_type = "weekday"),
  date = date, strata = day_type, survey_type = "bus_route",
  sampling_frame = frame, site = site, circuit = circuit,
  wait_time = wait_min, circuit_time = circuit_min, p_period = 0.5
)
design <- add_interviews(design, interviews,
  effort = trip_hours, catch = catch, trip_status = trip_status,
  n_counted = n_counted, n_interviewed = n_interviewed
)
#> Warning: ! No `n_anglers` provided — assuming 1 angler per interview.
#> ℹ Pass `n_anglers = <column>` to use actual party sizes for angler-hour
#>   normalization.
#> ℹ If the interviews really are one angler each, pass `n_anglers = 1` to state
#>   that and silence this warning.
#> ℹ 2 interviews have zero catch.
#>   Zero catch is usual; check it is not missing data recorded as 0.
#> ℹ Added 16 interviews: 16 complete (100%), 0 incomplete (0%)
effort <- estimate_effort(design)
effort$estimates
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>   estimate    se ci_lower ci_upper     n
#>      <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl> <int>
#> 1     827.     0     827.     827.    16
effort$unit
#> [1] "party-hours"

# Per day, in minutes: Pollock et al. print 24,814.80 from site terms rounded to two
# decimals; unrounded it is 24,816.
effort$estimates$estimate / 2 * 60
#> [1] 24816

catch <- estimate_total_catch(design)
# Per day: Pollock et al. print 227.88 from the rounded 0.633; unrounded it is 228.
catch$estimates$estimate / 2
#> [1] 228

The standard error is 0 only because the two entered days are identical, so there is no between-day variation to measure. It says nothing about Pollock et al.’s survey, which reports one day and no variance. tests/testthat/test-bus-route-wait-time.R checks both figures.

10. Why the Weights Matter

Each site’s contribution is divided by its πi\pi_i, so an error in πi\pi_i is an error in that site’s share of the total. Two common errors, on the Pollock et al. route above:

  • A fixed πi=0.5\pi_i = 0.5 for every site. That is not an inclusion probability of the design. Each site is then off by the ratio of 0.5 to its true πi\pi_i; site 1’s true πi\pi_i is 30/360×0.5=0.04230/360 \times 0.5 = 0.042, so it would be understated twelvefold.
  • Wait shares rescaled to add up to 1 (wi/∑ww_i / \sum w). Every total is multiplied by ∑w/T=195/360=0.54\sum w / T = 195/360 = 0.54: the 165 minutes of travel are treated as if they were spent watching.

  • Jones, C. M., & Pollock, K. H. (2012). Recreational angler survey methods: estimation of effort, harvest, and released catch. Chapter 19 in Fisheries Techniques (3rd ed.), pp. 883–919. American Fisheries Society.

  • Lumley, T. (2010). Complex Surveys: A Guide to Analysis Using R. Wiley.

  • Pollock, K. H., Jones, C. M., & Brown, T. L. (1994). Angler survey methods and their applications in fisheries management. American Fisheries Society Special Publication 25.

  • Robson, D., & Jones, C. M. (1989). The theoretical basis of an access site angler survey design. Biometrics, 45, 83–98.
